extra.message: No rate limiting on authentication endpoints enables brute force — Attackers can brute-force user passwords or enumerate valid email addresses at high speed, compromising accounts. [verified: Same deficiency as finding 1: all three sensitive auth endpoints (/login, /register, /password-reset/request) are completely unthrottled — no IP-based limiting, no CAPTCHA, no delay mechanism — leaving password brute-force and user enumeration unmitigated.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Brute-force password attacks against user accounts, account enumeration, and denial of service through excessive password-reset requests. [verified: No rate-limiting middleware, decorator, or dependency exists anywhere in the codebase (requirements.txt lacks any throttling library; main.py has no limiter middleware); the login, register, and password-reset endpoints accept unlimited requests, enabling brute-force password guessing and email enumeration at full speed.]

Password reset tokens written to cleartext log file — An attacker with access to the log file can read raw password reset tokens and take over any user account that has requested a password reset. [verified: Same sink as finding 0: auth.py line 182 appends the raw token (generate_token() output) plus email to `password_reset_tokens.log` before the raw value is discarded; the token stored in the DB is hashed but the cleartext log entry is a direct credential for account takeover.]

Cleartext Storage of Password Reset Tokens in Log File — Account takeover of any user who requests a password reset, if an attacker gains read access to the password_reset_tokens.log file. [verified: Line 182 of auth.py writes the raw (unhashed) password-reset token to `password_reset_tokens.log` with no environment guard; anyone with filesystem read access to this file can use the token to call /api/auth/password-reset/confirm and take over the account within the 1-hour validity window.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Password Reset Request Endpoint — Account enumeration, resource exhaustion, and denial of service via repeated requests [verified: No rate limiting exists anywhere in the codebase — no library, middleware, or per-endpoint throttle; the endpoint is publicly accessible and repeated requests enable timing-based enumeration and resource exhaustion despite the consistent 202 response.]

SSRF via DNS rebinding in webhook delivery — An attacker with ops_admin access can configure a webhook with a DNS-rebinding domain that resolves to an internal IP on the second lookup, enabling server-side requests to internal services. [verified: Same DNS rebinding TOCTOU in _is_safe_url (line 27 function definition) — the hostname IP check and the actual HTTP request use separate DNS resolutions with no interlock; both enqueue_event and test_webhook are affected when DISPATCH_WEBHOOKS_LIVE=1.]

SSRF via DNS Rebinding TOCTOU in Webhook URL Validation — Server-side request forgery to internal services and cloud metadata endpoints, enabling lateral movement and credential theft from internal infrastructure. [verified: _is_safe_url resolves the hostname once via socket.getaddrinfo (line 44) for IP validation, but urllib.request.urlopen re-resolves independently (line 83/119), creating a real TOCTOU gap exploitable via DNS rebinding — no IP pinning, caching, or other compensating control exists.]

Hardcoded default SECRET_KEY enables token forgery — An attacker can forge valid session cookies, password reset tokens, and API key hashes for any user, gaining full authenticated access. [verified: Same as finding 0 — the default SECRET_KEY 'dev-secret-do-not-use-in-production-this-is-long-enough' on config.py:9 drives token HMAC through hash_token() in security.py; .env override exists but the known default is reachable and forgeable absent operator intervention, with no production guard rejecting the default.]

Session cookie Secure flag defaults to False — Session cookies transmitted over plain HTTP can be intercepted by network attackers, enabling session hijacking. [verified: Same as finding 1 — cookie_secure: bool = False on config.py:13 controls the Secure flag in _set_session_cookie(); HttpOnly+SameSite=Lax reduce risk but do not eliminate cleartext session-cookie exposure when the flag defaults to false and no runtime enforcement exists.]

Hardcoded Default SECRET_KEY Enables Session Forgery — Complete authentication bypass — an attacker can forge session tokens for any user, including ops_admin, gaining full system access. [verified: The default SECRET_KEY 'dev-secret-do-not-use-in-production-this-is-long-enough' is hardcoded in config.py and used via hash_token() in security.py for HMAC-SHA256 session/password-reset/API-key hashing; pydantic_settings overrides from .env exist but no runtime guard rejects the known default if an operator fails to set the env var, making token forgery possible with that well-known value.]

Session Cookies Missing Secure Flag by Default — Session hijacking via network sniffing on unencrypted connections, allowing an attacker to impersonate authenticated users. [verified: cookie_secure defaults to False in config.py and is passed directly to Response.set_cookie() in _set_session_cookie() (auth.py line 37); the cookie already has HttpOnly+SameSite=Lax mitigations, but the Secure flag absent by default means session cookies transmit over cleartext HTTP when HTTPS is not enforced, and no runtime check requires Secure=true in production.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Password Reset Confirmation Endpoint — Token brute-forcing and denial of service via repeated confirmation attempts [verified: Rate limiting is absent on this public endpoint; token brute-force is cryptographically infeasible (256-bit random token, 1-hour expiry), but repeated invalid confirmations still enable resource-exhaustion/DoS with no throttle in place.]
